newsitem.title: THAILAND: FOCUS-Thai stocks plummet, baht stabilises.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Thai stocks plummet, baht stabilises.

text.p: Thai stocks plummeted on Monday on profit taking and mounting concerns about listed companies' foreign exchange losses following the flotation of the baht, brokers said.

The composite SET Index closed 24.06 points, or 3.66 percent, lower at 633.03 as investors took profits after last week's rally, which saw the index surge 24.4 percent following the de facto devaulation. Turnover was 10.13 billion baht ($355 million).
Brokers said the market was expected to remain volatile for the rest of the week as economic problems and concerns over non-performing loans in the finance sector persist

"Share prices have reached the level that investors viewed as the opportunity to take profit," said one analyst at United Securities. "There is also rising worry about most companies' foreign exchange loss."
The baht, which lost 15-20 percent last week after the surprise move to float the currency, was steady around 28.40/28.88 to the dollar on Monday.
Traders said the currency was supported by a comment from central bank governor Rerngchai Marakanond, who told reporters he saw the baht moving in a range of 27.50/28.50.
After the feeding frenzy of last week, stock brokers said investors were now sitting back and assessing the impact of the weaker baht on listed companies and the overall economy.

"The (stock) surge last week was due to bargain hunting after the baht uncertainty was removed, allowing foreigners to capitalise on foreign exchange gains. Now the market will sit back to assess the impact of the baht float," said Satit Wannasilapin of Capital Nomura Securities Plc.
Bank shares, led by Bangkok Bank Plc and Thai Farmers Bank Plc, dominated activity, accounting for 38.2 percent of total trade.
Shares in the two major banks, representing a combined 25.3 percent of market turnover, fell five baht and three baht, respectively.
Songglod Bhichaikul of United Securities Plc said foreign investors still remained bullish on discounted major Thai banks, buying them on the exchange's main board through local nominees.
But he warned that any fresh rallies would be selective, based on performance prospects of individual and sectoral stocks.
"We will probably not see sharp spurts and wild swings like last week. It is time to go down to corporate details including how much foreign exchange losses faced by listed companies," Songglod said.
Thailand is in its worst economic slump in more than a decade with its finance sector over-exposed to cash-strapped and glutted property firms.
Prior to the de facto devaluation, the SET index had slumped to its lowest level in eight years and the currency was under attack from speculators.

Analysts said companies benefiting from the baht's new regime, such as Thai Airways International Plc, would do well. Brokers estimated more than 70 percent of the airline's revenue is denominated in foreign currencies, which would translate into hefty foreign exchange gains.
However, jitters over the bourse's medium and long-term outlook sent warrants tumbling.

Analysts said electronics, energy and entertainment counters were poised for profit taking after advances last week, but banks and communications may further rebound after their sizeable retreats in recent months.
Songglod of United Securities saw the SET Index moving in the 630-680 range in the short-term.
